planting.note: Site divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil along shaded streambanks or seepage slopes.

directions: Site divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil along shaded streambanks or seepage slopes, the moist montane forest settings where this Pacific Northwest native fern is naturally found from British Columbia into Oregon. Unusual among sword ferns, mature plants often produce small bulblets near the frond tips that can be pegged down to root and propagate new plants, a distinctive trait worth watching for. Its large, once-pinnate evergreen fronds make it a good companion for lady fern and deer fern in cool, damp woodland plantings.

planting.note: Establish divisions in fall on rocky, well-drained slopes or open woodland in filtered shade.

directions: Establish divisions in fall on rocky, well-drained slopes or open woodland in filtered shade, the dry chaparral-edge and oak-woodland habitat this California and Oregon native occupies in the wild. It is the most drought-tolerant western Dryopteris, holding its leathery, twice-pinnate evergreen fronds through the long dry season with little irrigation once roots are established. Use it as a durable filler in dry-shade native plantings where more moisture-demanding wood ferns would struggle.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into shallow pockets of gritty, well-drained soil among rocks or in a crevice garden in spring.

directions: Tuck divisions into shallow pockets of gritty, well-drained soil among rocks or in a crevice garden in spring, echoing the cliffs and talus slopes this widespread western native inhabits from the Rockies to the Pacific Coast, with disjunct populations near the Great Lakes. The small, deciduous, twice-pinnate fronds die back cleanly in late summer heat and return reliably each spring, making it a tidy, low-water choice for rock gardens and dry shaded walls. It is best grown where winter and spring moisture are followed by a drier summer rest.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich soil over limestone or other calcareous rock, tucked into shaded ledges.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich soil over limestone or other calcareous rock, tucked into shaded ledges or the base of rock walls where this eastern and midwestern native naturally colonizes crevices and talus. The lacy, twice-pinnate deciduous fronds arise from a fertile, stabilized hybrid lineage between fragile fern and bulblet bladder fern, and it often self-sows modestly along suitable rock outcrops. It pairs well with walking fern and other calciphile species in a shaded limestone rock garden.
